research_recommendation:
Have learners review and reinforce these BIG IDEAS: 
Functions describe relationships between two things that vary. Understanding functions is strengthened when they are explored across representations (e.g., equations, tables, and graphs). 
Symbols, especially those involving equality and variables, must be well understood conceptually for students to be successful in mathematics.
Mathematical modeling is the process of using mathematics to analyze and provide insight into real-world issues, dimensions, and other phenomena
gold_activity:
Example of functions describe relationships
The Walking Clown problem
A Clown began walking a certain number of centimeters away from his home. Find out whether the clown walked a constant speed or not by examining the table. 
Total cm    time, sec
---------------------------
13.25          10
17.00          16
22.625        25
32.00          40
44 1/2         60
From the data table, learners may elaborate a graph and obtain an equation. In this example, the two things that vary are the distance, measured in cm and the time in seconds
Example of symbols must be well understood
Seven birds have landed in your backyard, some landed on a tree, and some are at your feeder. How many birds might be in the tree and how many at the feeder?
If I have t birds in the tree, how might you describe how many birds are at the feeder?
Students might answer:
"Seven minus t" (7-t)
If the students answer "f" (for the variable to represent the number of birds at the feeder), then ask how t and f are related in an equation
Three equations describe the situation: 
t+f=7
7-f=t
7-t=f
Example of modeling a real-world issue with mathematics:
Jane is in a walkathon. A rule or “function” tells us how much Jane will earn depending on how many kilometers she walks. We don't know what the function is. Assume it is a linear function. We do know that if Jane walks 1 kilometer she will earn 4 dollars and if she walks 3 kilometers she will earn 8 dollars. Figure out the slope of the function that tells how much Jane will earn.
Checked results: clown distance d=0.625t+7 cm for the listed observations; Jane earns E=2k+2 dollars under the linear-model assumption.

research_recommendation:
It is recommended to use a function machine to help students find relationships between inputs and outputs in data tables. A function machine consists in that students receive several input numbers and their corresponding output numbers, and the students are to conjecture what the machine is doing to the input numbers to produce the output numbers. Students then check their conjectures against all the number pairs they have and, if valid to that point, use one or two more input/output pairs as reinforcement of the relationship that they have discovered.
Another way that  students may investigate functions is by assuming the role of a “robot” that asks classmates to identify the relationship between two sets of data by identifying numeric patterns as a rule.

misconception: when students mistakenly switch variables when transposing expressions involving subtraction
research_recommendation:
Some learners have the erroneous idea that "You cannot take a bigger number from a smaller number", due to they hear this phrase as they first learn to subtract whole numbers. Students are restricted to only the set of whole numbers, subtracting a larger number from a smaller one results in a negative number, an integer that is not in the set of whole numbers, so this rule is true. Later, students encounter application or word problems involving contexts that include integers, students learn that this “rule” is not true for all problems.
Give learners exercises involving the subtraction of different types of numbers (whole numbers, decimals and fractions) that will produce negative numbers as result, then give them feedback when they find trouble.
gold_activity:
A grocery store manager keeps the temperature of the produce section at 4 degrees Celsius, but this is 22 degrees too hot for the frozen food section. What must the temperature be in the frozen food section? In this case, the answer is a negative number:
4º-22º=-18°

misconception: when students mistakenly switch variables when transposing expressions involving subtraction
research_recommendation: Apply with learners the "text-change paradigm", also known as the "change-detection paradigm". This paradigm consists in that students are given a text of some sort to read on a computer screen, and then they are presented with a second text that is either identical to the ﬁrst text or changed very slightly in some way. The task is for the learner to determine whether the second text is different or not, and if it is, to report how it is different. The idea is that changes that are noticed reﬂect deeper surface-level processing of the original text, whereas changes that are not noticed reﬂect shallow processing of surface features.  But rather than changing the text at the word level, make changes in the word order of the original text. When the ﬁrst text is shown in the less helpful order, it has to be changed in the second text to the helpful order and vice versa.

misconception: when students mistakenly perceive variables as labels or units, or associate their value with their alphabetical position
research_recommendation:
Reinforce in learners the key idea that letters in algebra don't have specific values that depend on their position in the alphabet.
For example, it is usual for teacher to say "Let L stand for the length" rather than the more complex statements "let L stand for the number of meters in the length" or "Let L stand for the number of meters long." Another compromising statement is: "Let the length be L meters" or "Let L be the length in meters", instead remark that L stands for a number and not for the word length. Solve problems with variables naming them correctly and using the correct expressions to denote that letters represent numbers.
gold_activity:
Example:
n stands for an unknown number. Write the following in mathematical symbols: 
Add 5 to n, then multiply by 3
Common learners' error:
1 + 5 = 6
6*3 = 18
Correct A:
(5 + n)*3

misconception: when students mistakenly perceive variables as labels or units, or associate their value with their alphabetical position
research_recommendation: Discuss different interpretations students give to letters: evaluated unknowns, quantities whose individual values need not be found, object labels, generalized numbers, and varying quantities. Distinguish labels such as a point named A from algebraic variables that represent numbers. In formulas, p can represent the numerical perimeter in a stated unit and A the numerical area in a stated square unit; the letters do not stand for physical objects. Ask learners which interpretation is appropriate in each context.
gold_activity:
Examples:
1) The letter is directly evaluated
x+6=12
x = ?

2) Technically do not have to evaluate - can ignore the letters altogether and just add 2 to 43, a + b + 2 = 45
a + b = 43 
a + b + 2 =? 

3) Distinguish object labels from numerical variables. A point can be named A. In a formula, p is the numerical perimeter in a stated unit and a is the numerical area in a stated square unit.

4) Letters stand for an unknown quantity that cannot be evaluated
Mary is 3 inches taller than Bob. Bob's height is denoted by b. Therefore, Mary's height is b + 3.

5) Letters can represent a set of numbers, instead of one specific  number
x + y < 20 
x>y
y=?

6) The relationship varies
Which is larger, 2n or n + 2? 
In this case, it depends on what n equals. 
If n = 0, then n + 2 is greater. 
If n = 3, 2n is greater

misconception: when students incorrectly assume two variables in an equation must represent distinct numerical values, rather than potentially representing the same expression
research_recommendation:
Make learners practice problem situations that support the convention where two variables can in fact be equivalent.
Allow students to elaborate tables listing the possible combination of both variables, as well as graphs showing their relationship and systematic drawings representing the context.
gold_activity:
For example:
Q: Ricardo has 8 pet mice. He keeps them in two cages that are connected so that the mice can go back and forth between the cages. One of the cages is blue, and the other is green. Show all the ways that 8 mice can be in two cages.
The situation can be represented by the equation b+g=8, where b is the number of mice in the blue cage and g is the number in the green cage.
Can b=g be true?
Learners usually answer: b can't be the same as g, because the letters represent different things
Correct A: b=g is true when there are 4 mice in each box, so b=g is true for number 4

misconception: when students incorrectly assume two variables in an equation must represent distinct numerical values, rather than potentially representing the same expression
research_recommendation: Start practicing with equations that are solvable and leaving until later those that have no solution. Make an introduction to equation solving that handles simultaneously an arithmetic identity and an equation.
gold_activity:
For example, ask students: 
"Can you use the equal sign with an operation on both sides?"
Learners could respond with an example involving commutativity such as
5*4 = 4*5
or
2+6 = 6+2
Then, ask: "Can you give me an example with a different operation on each side?"
It could be obtained expected answers such as 
5+5 = 5*2
but also unexpected ones such as 
0+0 = 0*0
Then ask: "Can you give me an example in which you have more than one operation on each side?"
Some of their answers can be:
2+2+2 = 2*3
4*3+1-3 = 3*2+4
3+5+4 = 12-4+4 
2+1*5 = 3*4−5

Ask specifically for examples using brackets and you'll probably obtain equalities such as these: 
(2+3)*5 = 3*5+2+8
2+(5*4)=3+7+12
(5+2)*3 = 2*10+1

research_recommendation:
Reinforce in learners the key idea that letters in algebra don't have specific values that depend on their position in the alphabet.
For example, it is usual for teacher to say "Let L stand for the length" rather than the more complex statements "let L stand for the number of meters in the length" or "Let L stand for the number of meters long." Another compromising statement is: "Let the length be L meters" or "Let L be the length in meters", instead remark that L stands for a number and not for the word length. Solve problems with variables naming them correctly and using the correct expressions to denote that letters represent numbers.

Example:
n stands for an unknown number. Write the following in mathematical symbols: 
Add 5 to n, then multiply by 3
Common learners' error:
1 + 5 = 6
6*3 = 18
Correct A:
(5 + n)*3

misconception: when students struggle to grasp that variables can represent changing or varying quantities
research_recommendation: Discuss different interpretations students give to letters: evaluated unknowns, quantities whose individual values need not be found, object labels, generalized numbers, and varying quantities. Distinguish labels such as a point named A from algebraic variables that represent numbers. In formulas, p can represent the numerical perimeter in a stated unit and A the numerical area in a stated square unit; the letters do not stand for physical objects. Ask learners which interpretation is appropriate in each context.
gold_activity:
Examples:
1) The letter is directly evaluated
x+6=12
x = ?

2) Technically do not have to evaluate - can ignore the letters altogether and just add 2 to 43, a + b + 2 = 45
a + b = 43 
a + b + 2 =? 

3) Distinguish object labels from numerical variables. A point can be named A. In a formula, p is the numerical perimeter in a stated unit and a is the numerical area in a stated square unit.

4) Letters stand for an unknown quantity that cannot be evaluated
Mary is 3 inches taller than Bob. Bob's height is denoted by b. Therefore, Mary's height is b + 3.

5) Letters can represent a set of numbers, instead of one specific  number
x + y < 20 
x>y
y=?

6) The relationship varies
Which is larger, 2n or n + 2? 
In this case, it depends on what n equals. 
If n = 0, then n + 2 is greater. 
If n = 3, 2n is greater

n stands for an unknown number. Write the following in mathematical symbols:

research_recommendation: Learners may have the wrong idea that "-x Is Negative x". For these students, then, -x means that the value of this expression will always be negative. This is problematic for students when x represents a negative number. If students consistently read the expression as the opposite of x, it would help them make sense of the expression. Make learners solve problems involving negative numbers and variables, calling them each time "the opposite of __" rather than "negative __". Ask learners to do the same way when they read expressions and work on solving algebra exercises.

For example, in an equation such as x+4=2, the students believe that it is impossible to find the negative value of x. Where the unknown is preceded by a minus sign, confusion arises regarding the sign of the solution. With equations such as 4-x=5 or -x=6, they are no longer sure if the minus sign is a subtraction sign  or if it is part of a negative number.

research_recommendation:
To help children focus on the commutative property, pair problems that have the same addends but in different orders. Using different contexts helps children focus on the significant similarities in the problems.

Note that students may attempt to overgeneralize the commutative property to subtraction. Use contextual situations or story problems to help them confront this misconception.

research_recommendation:
Some learners have the erroneous idea that "You cannot take a bigger number from a smaller number", due to they hear this phrase as they first learn to subtract whole numbers. Students are restricted to only the set of whole numbers, subtracting a larger number from a smaller one results in a negative number, an integer that is not in the set of whole numbers, so this rule is true. Later, students encounter application or word problems involving contexts that include integers, students learn that this “rule” is not true for all problems.
Give learners exercises involving the subtraction of different types of numbers (whole numbers, decimals and fractions) that will produce negative numbers as result, then give them feedback when they find trouble.
gold_activity:
A grocery store manager keeps the temperature of the produce section at 4 degrees Celsius, but this is 22 degrees too hot for the frozen food section. What must the temperature be in the frozen food section? In this case, the answer is a negative number:
4º-22º=-18°

For example, ask students: 
"Can you use the equal sign with an operation on both sides?"
Learners could respond with an example involving commutativity such as
5*4 = 4*5
or
2+6 = 6+2
Then, ask: "Can you give me an example with a different operation on each side?"

5+5 = 5*2
but also unexpected ones such as 
0+0 = 0*0

2+2+2 = 2*3
4*3+1-3 = 3*2+4
3+5+4 = 12-4+4 
2+1*5 = 3*4−5

Ask specifically for examples using brackets and you'll probably obtain equalities such as these: 
(2+3)*5 = 3*5+2+8
2+(5*4)=3+7+12
(5+2)*3 = 2*10+1

misconception: when students struggle with forming and understanding algebraic expressions and equations.
research_recommendation: Use equivalent equations to help students overcome confusion between operations in an algebraic expression, such as grouping similar terms, reducing and expanding fractions, and the transformations used to solve an equation.
gold_activity:
For example:
The equation (2x/3)-1=0 can be transformed into 2x-3=0
The algebraic expression (2x/3)-1 can be transformed into (2x-3)/3. 
A student who confuses the two concepts might incorrectly transform (2x/3)-1into 2x-3
It is important that students understand this difference

misconception: when students struggle with forming and understanding algebraic expressions and equations.
research_recommendation: Use diagrams and contexts to explain operation order. In conventional notation, multiplication and division have equal precedence and are evaluated left to right; addition and subtraction also share precedence and are evaluated left to right. Alternative orders are valid only after an equivalent rewrite: division by a nonzero number becomes multiplication by its reciprocal, and subtraction becomes addition of the opposite. For example, 30÷2×15÷3×4 = 30×(1/2)×15×(1/3)×4. Once written as a product, its factors may be regrouped and reordered.
gold_activity:
Rocky decided that it was time to move to new quarters, but the current state of his home would not fetch many acorns on the real estate market. Some home improvements were needed. The front walk was a good place to begin. Rocky wanted to make a new walkway consisting of 3 large squares, with each square being 4 paving stones across. How many paving stones will Rocky need to buy for his new walk?
Represent the story with an arithmetic expression. It must involve a power.
Learners usually get to the expression: 3*4^2
Some learners solve it to get 144 and others get 48
After drawing the situation, they realize the correct answer is 48 and so, the priority of powers makes sense in the hierarchy of operations

Example of changing the divisions by fractions:
30÷2*15÷3*4 becomes 30*(1/2)*15*(1/3)*4

misconception: when students struggle with forming and understanding algebraic expressions and equations.
research_recommendation:
Some learners may have the wrong idea that they have to multiply everything inside the parentheses by the number outside the parentheses. As students are developing the foundational skills linked to order of operations, they are often told to first perform multiplication on the numbers (terms) within the parentheses. This holds true only when the numbers or variables inside the parentheses are being added or subtracted, because the distributive property is being used. The rule is untrue when multiplication or division occurs in the parentheses. This error may not emerge in situations students encounter terms that do not involve the distributive property or students use the distributive property without the element of terms. The confusion seems to be an interaction between students’ partial understanding of terms and their partial understanding of the distributive property.
Make learners solve problems that involve this idea, then check if they apply it incorrectly and provide feedback.
gold_activity:
For example:
3(5+4)=3*5+3*4
In this case, the "rule" is true
2(4*9)≠2*4*2*9
In this case, the "rule" is untrue

Incorrect student chain: 2.30+3.20=5.50−1.50=4.00 
Since 2.30+3.20 equals 5.50, not 5.50-1.50, the string of equations they have written violates the definition of equality
Correct calculation: 2.30+3.20=5.50, then 5.50−1.50=4.00. Daniel originally had $4.00.

research_recommendation:
Some learners may have the wrong idea that "The equal sign means Find the answer or Write the answer".
An equal sign is a relational symbol. It indicates that the two quantities on either side of it represent the same amount. Make learners solve equations where they may see an equal sign that expresses the relationship, but cannot be interpreted as Find the answer.
gold_activity:

6=□+4
3+x=5+2x

misconception: when students neglect to check their solutions or make errors during the checking process
research_recommendation: If checking is taught, examples should be given of checking incorrect solutions as well. In the case of detection of a mistake, further action as to how to find out where exactly the mistake has been made and how to correct it should be discussed.
gold_activity:
Example
Solve for x: 4-x=5 and check your solution
Lerners' procedure: 
4-x=5
-x=5-4
-x=1
x=-1
Checking:
4-(-1)=?
Makes no sense! 

Correct A: 
x=-1
Checking: 
4-(-1)=4+1=5

research_recommendation:
Some learners may have the wrong idea that to check if two expressions are equivalent, substitute “1” for the variable because that Is the easiest.
Students are sometimes taught to routinely substitute an “easy” number for the variable. Often, that number is 0, 1, or 2. If the substitution method is used to determine equivalent expressions, multiple values should be used to avoid coincidental situations. However, the substitution method does not always lead to a correct decision regarding equivalence, because it depends on the values students choose. 
Have learners solve different problems involving equations, and check if the student has the tendency to substitute one "easy" number to find the solution, then provide feedback.
One counterexample disproves equivalence. Agreement at several chosen inputs is evidence, not a general proof; use valid algebraic transformations to establish an identity.
gold_activity:
For example, if the expressions are x^3 and x^2, and a student selects 0 and 1 to test, the resulting values could erroneously indicate that these expressions are equivalent. Using multiple values and not only those 0 and 1, will show that these expressions are not equivalent
For example, at x=2, x³=8 and x²=4. This single counterexample proves the expressions are not equivalent.

research_recommendation: Ask learners to solve exercises with the intention to make them check their solution, then use cognitive model tracing by dynamically generating the plausible steps, checking them against student’s solution steps and intervening when errors occur. Monitor the student’s mastery of knowledge from problem to problem, meaning the various cognitive skills. As far as the student’s solution remains on a correct path, remain silent to let the student continue working out. Otherwise, provide feedback as soon as an error occurs.If needed, provide help for the correct step(s) upon student request.

2x - 1 = -2 + 5x
Student's procedure:
2x - 1 = -2 + 5x

4x    =    5x

x = 1/3
Checking:
2(1/3) - 1 = -2 + 5(1/3)
2/3 - 1 = -2 + 5/3
Left side: 2/3−1=−1/3. Right side: −2+5/3=−1/3. Both sides agree.

research_recommendation:
Some learners may have the wrong idea that "The number you say first in counting is always less than the number that comes next".
In the early development of number, students are regularly encouraged to think that number relationships are fixed. For example, the relationship between 3 and 8 is always the same. To determine the relationship between two numbers, the numbers must implicitly represent a count made by using the same unit. But when units are different, these relationships change.
Have learners compare quantities after converting to common units, and compare signed numbers on a number line. The numerical fact 3<8 remains true; quantities such as 3 dozen and 8 individual items are different comparisons
gold_activity:
As numbers, 3<8 always. Quantities with different units, or the different numbers −3 and −8, require their own comparisons.

misconception: when students get confusion over operation symbols and their meanings in algebra
research_recommendation: Learners may have the wrong idea that "-x Is Negative x". For these students, then, -x means that the value of this expression will always be negative. This is problematic for students when x represents a negative number. If students consistently read the expression as the opposite of x, it would help them make sense of the expression. Make learners solve problems involving negative numbers and variables, calling them each time "the opposite of __" rather than "negative __". Ask learners to do the same way when they read expressions and work on solving algebra exercises.
gold_activity:
For example, in an equation such as x+4=2, the students believe that it is impossible to find the negative value of x. Students also attempt to avoid negative solutions to equations, involving, for example, changing the structure of an equation or a problem definition in order to obtain a positive solution.
Where the unknown is preceded by a minus sign, confusion arises regarding the sign of the solution. With equations such as 4-x=5 or -x=6, they are no longer sure if the minus sign is a subtraction sign  or if it is part of a negative number.

research_recommendation: Apply with learners the "text-change paradigm", also known as the "change-detection paradigm". This paradigm consists in that students are given a text of some sort to read on a computer screen, and then they are presented with a second text that is either identical to the ﬁrst text or changed very slightly in some way. The task is for the learner to determine whether the second text is different or not, and if it is, to report how it is different. The idea is that changes that are noticed reﬂect deeper surface-level processing of the original text, whereas changes that are not noticed reﬂect shallow processing of surface features.  But rather than changing the text at the word level, make changes in the word order of the original text. When the ﬁrst text is shown in the less helpful order, it has to be changed in the second text to the helpful order and vice versa.

research_recommendation:
Guide learners to develop a "check-as-you-go" strategy when solving word problems that require translating from common language to algebraic sentences and that may produce a reversal order error, either additive or multiplicative.
This check-as-you-go strategy is deployed by students, triggering a self-correcting mechanism as students proceed through a set of similar problems. Make learners practice and practice with similar word problems, until they develop their own strategy to go checking their procedure as they work. Start with the "text-change paradigm", where learners are given different statements of the same problem, one more helpful than the other and, once learners have practiced enough in detecting which is the most helpful statement to solve a problem, give them more problems with one single statement and ask them to solve it the best way they can. Learners will probably use the strategy to change the statement themselves, and will develop by their own the check-as-you-go strategy so solve problems.

n + n = 76
76/2 = 38
n = 38
Students use to solve this equation correctly, using singletons (letter n alone) prior to grouped terms, such as 2n=76

research_recommendation: Avoid using key words to solve problems. Check if students use them, then provide feedback explaining them that keywords can be informative but must be used in conjunction with all other words in the problem to grasp the full meaning
gold_activity:
John had 14 marbles in his left pocket. He had 37 marbles in his right pocket. How many marbles did John have?
If students use keywords, they will subtract without realizing that the problem context requires addition to solve. Keywords become particularly troublesome students begin to explore multi step word problems, because they must decide which keywords work with which component of the problem
Correct answer: 14+37=51 marbles. Here “left” names a pocket; it does not mean subtract.
